Anatomy of Radical Musar: The Doctrine, Work, and Legacy of the Saba of Novhardok

This text surveys the life history and doctrine of Rabbi Yosef Yozel Horowitz, known as "the Saba of Novhardok," who led a radical and original stream within the Musar movement. The source details the Saba's transition from the world of commerce to total devotion to Torah, while presenting the unique educational approach of the Novhardok yeshiva based on breaking character traits, absolute trust in God, and renunciation of social esteem. The central chapter of the text analyzes his book "Madregat ha-Adam" (The Level of Man), which constitutes the ideological foundation for intensive soul-work, and compares his method to alternative approaches such as that of Slobodka or the Hazon Ish. Finally, the article describes the geographical expansion of the network throughout Europe and the restoration of the legacy in the Land of Israel after the destruction of the communities in the Holocaust.

Anatomy of Radical Musar: The Doctrine, Work, and Legacy of the Saba of Novhardok

The Life History of Rabbi Yosef Yozel Horowitz and the Course of His Spiritual Development

Rabbi Yosef Yozel Horowitz, known as the "Saba of Novhardok," was born in the year 5610 (1850) in the town of Plungyan in Lithuania (some sources mention his birth in the year 5608 in the town of Kurtovyan) to his father the Gaon Rabbi Shlomo Zalman Horowitz (or Ziv), who was the town rabbi.[1, 2, 3, 4] In his youth, Rabbi Yosef Yozel was distinguished by brilliant and scholarly talents.[2, 4] At age eighteen he married a daughter of the town of Shveksna, but between his betrothal and marriage his father-in-law died, and the burden of supporting the extended family—including his wife's sisters—was placed entirely on his young shoulders.[2, 4] Out of commitment to his family, he turned to engage in commerce and traveled frequently for his business to the port city of Klaipėda (Memel).[2, 4] There, in a chance but fateful encounter, he met the founder of the Musar movement, Rabbi Yisrael of Salant.[2, 4] When Rabbi Yisrael asked him what he was engaged in, Rabbi Yosef Yozel replied that he must support his family.[2] Rabbi Yisrael persuaded him to devote most of his time to Torah study and invited him to a musar lesson, an encounter that captivated his heart and led him to completely abandon the world of commerce and devote himself to Torah and musar in the kollel his teacher had established in Kovno.[2, 5] Subsequently he studied and was among the disciples of Rabbi Avraham Shinker and Rabbi Simcha Zisel Ziv, "the Saba of Kelm."[2, 3, 5]

Out of a desire for complete detachment from the material world and its temptations, Rabbi Yosef Yozel imposed extreme asceticism upon himself and secluded himself in a small house in Slobodka for one year and nine months, without allowing anyone to enter.[2, 5] This seclusion aroused criticism from "the Saba of Kelm," who discovered the location of his dwelling and rebuked him that in times of spiritual crisis a person must not isolate himself alone but must go out and influence the world.[2, 4, 5] Rabbi Yosef Yozel accepted his teacher's words, returned to the community, and began to conduct journeys to various Jewish communities, where he established study halls that combined Gemara and musar study with financing from the benefactor Ovadiah Lachman of Berlin.[2, 5] In the year 5656 (1896) he founded the Novhardok yeshiva in the city of Novhardok in the district of Minsk.[4, 6] The yeshiva began with only ten students, and within a few months numbered some fifty young men.[2, 6] Its musar approach aroused fierce opposition from elements in the city who demanded the closure of the institution and appealed to the city rabbi, the Gaon Rabbi Yechiel Michel Halevi Epstein (author of "Arukh ha-Shulhan"), but he and the city leaders provided full support for the yeshiva.[2, 6] In its first ten years, Rabbi Eliyahu Dov Barkovsky served as mashgiach, and in 1899 the number of students reached two hundred.[6] In 1908, with the death of Rabbi Epstein and a fierce dispute that erupted in the city over the succession to the rabbinical position, the rosh yeshiva transferred two-thirds of the students to the city of Zhytel to prevent them from taking part in the political confrontations, and they returned only after the dispute subsided.[2, 6] In 1912 a new two-story building was inaugurated for the yeshiva.[6]

With the outbreak of World War I, out of concern about the influences of secularization and Haskalah that were widespread under German rule, the yeshiva relocated to Gomel and additional branches opened in Bobruisk, Mazyr, Orsha, and Rostov-on-Don.[6] In Gomel, Rabbi Yosef Yozel studied Kabbalah for two months with the kabbalist Rabbi Shlomo Elyashiv (author of the "Leshem").[5] In 1919 he moved to Kiev to assist the many refugees who flooded the city in harsh conditions.[2, 5] Following the outbreak of a typhus epidemic in the city, Rabbi Yosef Yozel cared for the sick with self-sacrifice, contracted the disease, and died on 17 Kislev 5680 (9 December 1919).[5, 6] His bones were later brought to Jerusalem and he was buried on Har ha-Menuhot.[2, 3, 4] His public and family legacy was perpetuated through his distinguished sons-in-law: Rabbi Avraham Yaffen, rosh yeshiva of Novhardok; Rabbi Raphael Alter Shmuelevitz, rabbi of Stutchin (father of Rabbi Chaim Shmuelevitz, rosh yeshiva of Mir); Rabbi Yisrael Yaakov Lubchansky, mashgiach at Ohel Torah yeshiva in Baranovichi; and Rabbi Reuven Silver (Shlivansky).[3]

After his death, the network continued to operate under Soviet rule, while suffering severe persecution from the Yevsektsiya.[5, 6] The rosh yeshiva in Gomel and ten students were arrested and sent to forced labor, which led to a bold decision in 1921 to smuggle all the students of the network across the Polish border in the midst of the Polish-Soviet War.[6] Rabbi Avraham Yaffen traveled to Kiev despite the dangers of the journey to strengthen the students, and in Kislev 5681 the first assembly without the "Saba" was held in Gomel, at which Rabbi Avraham assumed the spiritual leadership of the movement, which achieved tremendous expansion in Poland and in the Land of Israel.[5, 6]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Ideological Vision: "To Raise Complete Jews" and the Solution to the Spiritual Rupture

The central idea of Rabbi Yosef Yozel Horowitz was based on the aspiration to raise Jews who are complete in spirit and soul, who know the laws of the Creator and His Torah, possessors of upright hearts who seek "the true point" in all their actions.[5] They must be spiritual heroes, strong of soul and courageous of will, whom no storm of the world can move from their place.[5] Rabbi Yosef Yozel identified that in the past the world and the yeshiva complemented each other, but with time a deep abyss opened between the sacred and the profane, and the fire of holiness and enthusiasm cooled even within the yeshivot themselves.[5]

The solution that Novhardok proposed for this rupture was the elevation of the yeshivot and the restoration of their strength to the days of old, as it was in the golden age of the Babylonian exile in Sura and Pumbedita.[5] The path to achieving this goal required absolute devotion of the yeshiva members to the study of Torah and its commandments, while adopting musar methods that encompass all areas of life out of an aspiration to create a unique world of Torah from which the entire world would be built and influenced.[5] At the foundation of this conception stood the negation of natural human reason; Rabbi Yosef Yozel believed that man's reason serves as an instrument for distancing him from true self-work through excuses and personal biases, and therefore a person must subjugate his reason in every possible way and work on character traits in a practical and physical manner.[2, 6]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The Educational Methodology: The Study Regimen and Practical Work in Va'adim

Education in the Novhardok yeshivot presented exceptional diligence and close integration between intensive Torah study and practical musar work.[5] The study regimen, as it was conducted in the Białystok yeshiva—which was the largest among the movement's yeshivot—is characterized by a sequence of extended study hours into the night.[5, 6]

The Daily Schedule at the Białystok Yeshiva

The yeshiva was organized in va'adim that were managed by the senior students who excelled in education and musar work, including Rabbi Nisan Potashinsky, Rabbi Itzik Graybski, Rabbi Aharon Ogulnik, Rabbi Yaakov Zeldin, and Rabbi Yitzchak Elchanan Valdshan.[5] The educational process was divided into two main areas: practical work
The mussar instruction encompassed acquisition of knowledge in the works of the Rishonim such as Ḥovot ha-Levavot, the Rambam, Rabbenu Yonah, early biblical commentators like Ibn Ezra and Ramban, and the study of midrashim; alongside practical work in the domain of character traits and fear of Heaven according to the periods of the year.[5]

Practical character-trait work in committees according to the periods of the year

The book "Madregat ha-Adam": The writing project and the monthly study curriculum

The central composition of Rabbi Joseph Yozel, "Madregat ha-Adam" (Level of Man), contains the essence of the spiritual teaching of the Novhardok stream.[5] The process of creating the book began when Rabbi Joseph Yozel's students felt a need to commit his discourses to writing.[5] Rabbi Joseph Yozel would deliver his essays, and distinguished students would transcribe his words immediately during the session.[5] Subsequently, he would review the transcriptions, select the one who most precisely captured his intended thought—usually Rabbi Isaac Elḥanan Waldshan—and would correct, modify, add or delete until approving the essay.[5] In cases where he was not satisfied with the manner of writing, Rabbi Joseph Yozel would write the entire matter himself.[5]

After Rabbi Joseph Yozel's death, his essays were studied regularly in the Novhardok yeshiva network according to the months of the year, with each month focusing on a different booklet (essay) according to a fixed annual cycle.[5]

The structure of the book "Madregat ha-Adam" and the monthly study curriculum

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

The radical praxis: Breaking character traits, absolute trust, and the song of the narrow bridge

Novhardok championed a series of actions of "breaking character traits," the most notorious of which were acts of public self-abasement.[2] The purpose of these actions was to uproot from the student's heart the fear of environmental criticism, to strike at the inflated ego, and to develop absolute indifference to one's personal honor.[2, 7] For this reason, Novhardok students customarily dressed intentionally at first in worn and unrefined garments, and performed actions considered strange in the eyes of others, such as entering a pharmacy for the purpose of purchasing nails.[2, 6]

Another foundational principle was absolute trust in the Holy One, Blessed be He, while minimizing material effort to the absolute minimum.[1] Rabbi Joseph Yozel was confident and secure that his deficiencies would be filled if God so desired, and he did not exert himself for them at all.[1] A classic example of this is brought in the story of Rabbi Joseph Yozel who sat and secluded himself in a special house in the heart of the forest and engaged in Torah study.[1] When his candle gradually went out, he was distressed over the nullification of Torah study that would result, but he placed his trust in the Holy One, Blessed be He, that if light was due to him, it would be provided.[1] According to Novhardok tradition, his needs were indeed supplied to him beyond the bounds of nature.[2]

Seclusion in forests and isolated places ("beḍidut") was very common among the students for the purpose of acquiring the trait of trust and deepening ethical contemplation.[2, 5] This practice aroused discussions around the kabbalistic admonition of the Ari, of blessed memory, according to which one should not walk alone to places where there are no people.[8] Therefore, it became customary in some communities—particularly in Breslav Hasidism, which maintained a certain ideological affinity with Novhardok—to go to seclusion in pairs to the same place, with each one occupying a separate corner and secluding himself there between himself and his Creator.[8]

In this context, the most widespread song in the Novhardok yeshiva network was "The entire world is a very narrow bridge, and the essential thing is not to be afraid at all."[4] This song was composed by Rabbi Joseph Yozel himself, based on the famous saying of Rabbi Naḥman of Breslav in Likkutei Moharan, and it reflected the fearlessness and iron determination required of the yeshiva students in the face of life's hardships and the upheavals of the generation.[4]

--------------------------------------------------------------------------------

Dialectical analysis: Comparison, critique, and geographic expansion

Novhardok's teaching developed through constant dialectical confrontation with parallel ethical and halakhic conceptions in its generation, which deepened its uniqueness and sharpened its characteristics.[6, 9]

Dialectical comparison between the Novhardok method and the Slobodka method

In contrast, fierce opposition to this method came from the Gaon Rabbi Avraham Yeshayahu Karelitz ("the Ḥazon Ish").[9] The Ḥazon Ish opposed in principle the path of institutional mussar teaching, as well as the yeshiva study method that was based on the systems of Rabbi Ḥayyim of Brisk and Rabbi Shimon Shkop, since in his view these systems empower the learner's status as an autonomous subject over his subordination to the halakhic text.[9] The Ḥazon Ish did not recognize the human capacity to effect internal change arising from oneself alone, and therefore held that the only way to overcome the evil inclination is through absolute subordination to halakha and deep analytical Torah study.[9] The Ḥazon Ish saw Torah study itself as the instrument that subdues and breaks a person's character traits, without need for external psychological systems.[9] Nevertheless, it is worth noting that despite the ideological controversy, the Ḥazon Ish displayed practical patronage toward the network, and in 1936 even assisted in establishing the Novhardok married scholars' kollel "Ateret Yosef" in Bnei Brak (later transferred to Tel Aviv) in memory of the Grandfather of Novhardok.[6]

From a psychological perspective, Novhardok's extreme character-trait work sometimes exacted heavy prices.[7] The constant effort to accept insults and contempt led some students to a severe feeling of personal worthlessness and loss of meaning, which severely damaged their self-confidence and joy of life, and left them at times as "broken vessels" from excessive humiliations.[7] However, the iron resilience acquired by those who survived this crucible enabled the network to recover rapidly after World War I and to establish an extensive network of branches throughout Poland and Latvia.[6]

Branches of the "Bet Yosef" network in Poland and Latvia between the wars

The outbreak of World War II brought an end to the network's flourishing in Europe.[6] The students fled to Vilna and from there wandered to Birzhai.[6] Some received entry visas to the United States and established a branch there under the leadership of Rabbi Avraham Yaffen, while those who refused Soviet citizenship were sent to forced labor in Siberia.[6] Part of those remaining in Europe, including Rabbi Isaac Elḥanan Waldshan, were murdered by the Germans.[6] The Siberian survivors established a yeshiva in Łódź in 1946, and after the Kielce pogrom immigrated to the Land of Israel and integrated into local branches already established in the 1930s[6]:

Yeshivat "Bet Yosef" in Tel Aviv: Established in 1929 by Rabbi Hillel Vitkind, it moved to Bnei Brak in the 1960s and became the kollel "Bet Hillel" headed by his son-in-law Rabbi Mordekhai Man, and subsequently a yeshiva for young men named "Divrei Mordekhai" opened in the building under the leadership of his son Rabbi Joseph Man.[6]

Yeshivat "Bet Yosef" in Bnei Brak: Established in 1931 by Rabbi Mattityahu Shtigel with the assistance of Rabbi David Bliakher, and headed by Rabbi Ya'akov Yisrael Kanievsky ("the Steipler").[6]

Kollel "Ateret Yosef" and Kollel "Etz Yosef": Kollel Ateret Yosef was established in Tel Aviv and Bnei Brak, and in the 1940s was presided over by Rabbi Shemuel Weintraub, with one of its heads being Rabbi Shemaryahu Yosef Karelitz.[6] Rabbi Weintraub also served as president of Kollel "Etz Yosef" in Jerusalem, which was headed by his son-in-law Rabbi Isaac Bernstein.[6]

Yeshivat "Bet Yosef-Novhardok" in Jerusalem: Established in 1937 by Rabbi Ben-Zion Bruk, thereby sealing the enterprise of restoring the Novhardok heritage in the Holy Land.[6]
